Council feedback from openai_reviewer:
- candidate_trace_report.profile.muscles[muscle_id="muscle.zygomaticus_major.left"]: The tracer assigns a stabilizer role (0.25) to facial musculature. The demonstrated one-arm push-up and its stated anti-extension, anti-rotation, shoulder, elbow, scapular, and postural demands do not biomechanically support zygomaticus major as a movement stabilizer. Suggested correction: In a future revision, constrain stabilization tracing to muscles anatomically relevant to the stated joint and trunk/limb stabilization demands; exclude facial, ocular, laryngeal, and other unrelated muscles.
- candidate_trace_report.profile.muscles[muscle_id="muscle.ary_epiglottic_part_of_oblique_arytenoid.left"]: The tracer assigns a stabilizer role (0.25) to laryngeal musculature, an anatomically unrelated pattern that is not supported by the exercise instructions or frames. This is representative of the materially overbroad profile: 408 of 466 muscles are labeled stabilizers, including unrelated facial, ocular, pharyngeal, pelvic, and distal muscles. Suggested correction: In a future revision, repair the postural-stabilization mapping so it does not indiscriminately activate the broad anatomical catalog.
- candidate_trace_report.profile.muscles[muscle_id="muscle.lateral_head_of_triceps_brachii.left"]: The unilateral one-hand-supported movement is traced with equal primary activation for both left and right triceps heads (and likewise for both sides of pectoralis major). A single repetition uses one working arm; the source does not support simultaneous bilateral primary upper-limb recruitment. Suggested correction: In a future revision, make primary-mover output conditional on the selected working side, or represent an unspecified-side exercise without labeling both sides as concurrently primary.

assumptions: One arm works per set. It is represented as unilateral with the right side working, and the other side is performed as a separate set.
The concentric phase is pushing from the bottom (chest near or touching the floor) to a fully extended working arm, as the instructions describe.
The working humerus moves toward the midline across the chest from a partly flared elbow position, so the shoulder action is modeled as horizontal adduction, not pure sagittal flexion.
The scapula protracts as the arm pushes the torso away from the floor.
Because only one hand and two feet support the body, the trunk must resist both sagging into extension and rotating toward the unsupported side.
The wider foot stance is a base-of-support adjustment and adds no prime-mover joint actions.
The free arm rests passively behind the back and adds no meaningful joint action or demand.
Body weight is the only load, and performance is counted in repetitions.
classification_reasons: The instructions and both frames show a prone, closed-chain push-up with body weight supported on the toes and one hand, with the free hand behind the back.
The exertion phase is elbow extension combined with shoulder horizontal adduction and scapular protraction, all of which the vocabulary can represent.
Unilateral laterality lets the tracer count limb actions only on the working side, which addresses reviewer feedback that both triceps and pectoralis major were marked as primary movers.

No standing or postural_stabilization demand is used. Under the current tracer rules, face, eye, jaw, tongue, palate, pharynx and larynx muscles are always zero, which addresses feedback about facial and laryngeal stabilizers.

instructions: Begin laying prone on the ground. Move yourself into a position supporting your weight on your toes and one arm. Your working arm should be placed directly under the shoulder, fully extended. Your legs should be extended, and for this movement you may need a wider base, placing your feet further apart than in a normal push-up.
Maintain good posture, and place your free hand behind your back. This will be your starting position.
Lower yourself by allowing the elbow to flex until you touch the ground.
Descend slowly, and reverse direction be extending the arm to return to the starting position.
source.name: Single-Arm Push-Up
